t.3.57.1: Then Rāma, the delight of the Raghus, tormented by grief, questioned Saumitri again as he met him on the way, returning from the hermitage.
t.3.57.2: He said to him: "Why have you come here, abandoning Maithilī, when I left her in the forest trusting in you?"
t.3.57.3: The very moment I saw you arrive, Lakṣmaṇa, having left Maithilī behind, my mind, fearing some great evil, became truly troubled.
t.3.57.4: My left eye throbs, and so do my arm and my heart, O Lakṣmaṇa, as I see you far off on the path without Sītā.
t.3.57.5: Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, bearer of auspicious marks, again overcome with grief, spoke to the sorrowing Rāma.
t.3.57.6: It was not of my own will and choice that I left her and came here; driven by her own fierce words, I have come here to you.
t.3.57.7: That cry, "Ah Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa! Save me!", shouted as if by the noble one himself, reached the ears of Maithilī.
t.3.57.8: Hearing that cry of distress, Maithilī, out of her love for you, weeping and overwhelmed with fear, said to me, "Go! Go!"
t.3.57.9: Urged by her again and again with the word “Go!”, I answered Maithilī with these words, full of trust in you:
t.3.57.10: I see no rākṣasa who could bring fear upon him. Be at ease; this is not so. Someone has merely cried out in this way.
t.3.57.11: O Sītā, how could the noble one utter the contemptible and base words "Save me!", he who could save even the thirty gods?
t.3.57.13: Enough of giving yourself over to despair; be at ease and free from anxiety. There is no man in the three worlds, whether already born or yet being born, who could defeat Rāghava in battle, in combat.
t.3.57.14: Thus addressed, Vaidehī, her mind utterly bewildered, shedding tears, spoke to me these cruel words.
t.3.57.12: For some reason or other, someone imitating my brother's voice uttered in a distorted tone the words, 'Lakṣmaṇa, save me!' You should not give way to distress, which is the habit of base women.
t.3.57.15: An exceedingly sinful feeling toward me has been harbored by you; but even when your brother has perished and that moment has come, you shall never win me.
t.3.57.16: You follow Rāma by a secret pact with Bharata, for though he cries out so desperately, you do not go to him.
t.3.57.17: You are an enemy moving about in disguise, following along for my sake; seeking an opening against Rāghava, you therefore do not go to him.
t.3.57.18: Thus addressed by Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, agitated, his eyes red and his lips trembling with anger, went forth from the hermitage.
t.3.57.19: To Saumitri, who was speaking thus, Rāma, bewildered by anguish, said: "It was ill done, gentle one, that you have come here without her."
t.3.57.20: Even though you knew that I am capable of warding off the rākṣasas, you came out here, driven by these angry words of Maithilī.
t.3.57.21: Indeed, I am not pleased with you, for you have come away, abandoning Maithilī, and because, having heard harsh words from an angry woman, you have come here.
t.3.57.22: In every way this was a wrong deed on your part, that, urged on by Sītā and falling under the sway of anger, you did not carry out my command.
t.3.57.23: For yonder lies the rākṣasa, struck down by me with an arrow, by whom, in the form of a deer, I was drawn away from the hermitage.
t.3.57.24: Drawing my bow and fitting an arrow to it, I struck him with a shaft loosed as if in play; and that rākṣasa, casting off his deer's body, became a demon wearing armlets, crying out in a faltering voice.
t.3.57.25: It was that most dreadful utterance, spoken then in an anguished voice by the one struck by the arrow, who took on my own voice so that it carried far, because of which you have come here, abandoning Maithilī.
